docs.title: taxsim-py
docs.text: Federal income tax, payroll tax and state income tax for household records, as a Polars-first Python package. It follows NBER TAXSIM's inputs and meanings but is independent of, and not affiliated with, NBER.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
pip install taxsim-py                    # Python 3.9 or newer
pip install "taxsim-py[readstat]"        # also read and write Stata, SPSS and SAS files

On platforms without a prebuilt compiled calculator, pass engine="python" (slower).

docs.title: One household
docs.text:
from taxsim_py import calculate_row

result = calculate_row({"year": 2023, "state": 5, "mstat": 2, "page": 40, "pwages": 80_000})
result["fiitax"], result["siitax"], result["fica"]
# (5836.0, 1287.36, 12240.0)

The result is a plain dict: your inputs plus the results. state is the TAXSIM state code (5 is California; 0 means no state tax) and mstat is the filing status (2 is married filing jointly).

docs.title: Many households (a dataframe)
docs.text:
import polars as pl
from taxsim_py import calculate_taxes

households = pl.DataFrame(
    {
        "year": [2021, 2021],
        "state": [6, 36],       # TAXSIM codes: 6 Colorado, 36 Ohio
        "mstat": [1, 2],        # single, married filing jointly
        "page": [45, 50],
        "pwages": [50_000, 80_000],
        "swages": [0, 40_000],
        "depx": [0, 2],
    }
)

taxes = calculate_taxes(households)
taxes.select("fiitax", "siitax", "fica")

The result is the input, unchanged and in order, plus the output columns. Rows can mix states and years. Inputs you leave out count as zero; only mstat, state and the year are required.

docs.title: A file
docs.text:
From Python, scan the file with Polars and pass it in. A LazyFrame works as well as a DataFrame; the result is an eager DataFrame.

import polars as pl
from taxsim_py import calculate_taxes

taxes = calculate_taxes(pl.scan_parquet("households.parquet"))
taxes.write_parquet("taxes.parquet")

From the command line, with any of the supported file types:

taxsim-py households.csv taxes.csv

docs.title: In the browser
docs.text: The calculator is a form and CSV upload that runs the same code locally in the page through Pyodide; see Browser.

docs.title: What is supported
docs.text:
• Years: federal tax 1960-2025, state tax 1977-2025. Other years raise an error.
  • States: all 50 states and DC. States without an income tax return 0.
  • Inputs: all of TAXSIM's inputs, with the same meanings and units (Inputs).
  • Speed: a million mixed-state rows with marginal rates take about 7 seconds (Performance).

docs.title: Browser
docs.text:
Open the calculator. It runs taxsim-py in the page through Pyodide, in a web worker. Nothing is sent to a server.

  • One household: a form grouped like TAXSIM's, with marginal rates, detailed worksheets and calculation mode as options.
  • Upload a file: a CSV with one household per row (needs state, mstat and year, or set the year on the page), a preview of the results and a CSV download. The calculation runs in a web worker, so the page stays responsive, but very large files still need browser memory; use the command line for those.

docs.title: calculate_row
docs.text:
calculate_row(record: Mapping[str, Any], **options) -> dict

One household in, one dict out. record maps input names to values; options are any of the keyword options of calculate_taxes below.

from taxsim_py import calculate_row

calculate_row({"year": 2023, "state": 5, "mstat": 1, "pwages": 60_000}, mtr=85)

It builds a one-row dataframe and calls calculate_taxes, so for more than a handful of households use calculate_taxes directly.

docs.title: calculate_taxes
docs.text:
calculate_taxes(df, *, year=None, mtr=None, idtl=None, ...) -> pl.DataFrame

df is a Polars DataFrame or LazyFrame. The result is an eager DataFrame: the input, unchanged and in order, plus the output columns.

from taxsim_py import calculate_taxes

calculate_taxes(households)

docs.title: Options
docs.text: Everything below is a keyword argument, and each is optional.

docs.title: Which year, which state coding
docs.text:
Option Default Meaning year the year column Use this tax year for every row. Without it the frame needs a year column, and rows may mix years. year_column "year" Name of the year column. state_column "state" Name of the state column. state_id_type "taxsim" "taxsim" (codes 1-51, 0 for no state) or "fips" (Census state FIPS codes). 
calculate_taxes(df, year=2024)
calculate_taxes(df, state_id_type="fips")   # state=6 is California, not Colorado

docs.title: Marginal rates: mtr
docs.text:
mtr adds frate (federal) and srate (state) marginal rates, in percent, with respect to one kind of income or deduction. Pass a MarginalInput or TAXSIM's own numeric code, or put an integer mtr column in the frame to choose per row. 0 means no rates.

from taxsim_py import MarginalInput

calculate_taxes(df, mtr=MarginalInput.PRIMARY_WAGES)   # same as mtr=85
MarginalInput Code MarginalInput Code NONE 0 OTHER_PROPERTY_INCOME 79 BOTH_WAGES 11 PRIMARY_UNEMPLOYMENT 82 DIVIDENDS 12 PRIMARY_WAGES 85 INTEREST_RECEIVED 14 SPOUSE_WAGES 86 PRIMARY_SELF_EMPLOYMENT_INCOME 17 SOCIAL_SECURITY_BENEFITS 91 PENSIONS 20 RENT_PAID 160 NONPROPERTY_INCOME 30 SPOUSE_UNEMPLOYMENT 180 TRANSFERS 41 PRIMARY_BUSINESS_INCOME 211 PROPERTY_TAX 51 PRIMARY_PROFESSIONAL_INCOME 212 OTHER_ITEMIZED_DEDUCTIONS 54 S_CORPORATION_INCOME 213 MORTGAGE_INTEREST 56 SPOUSE_BUSINESS_INCOME 214 CHILDCARE_EXPENSES 64 SPOUSE_PROFESSIONAL_INCOME 215 SHORT_TERM_CAPITAL_GAINS 68 LONG_TERM_CAPITAL_GAINS 70

Marginal rates cost extra calculations, so leave mtr off when you do not need them.

docs.title: Detail: idtl, taxsim_names, keep_intermediate
docs.text:
• idtl=2 (or an idtl column holding 2) adds the federal and state worksheet lines with descriptive names, such as federal_taxable_income and state_adjusted_gross_income. See Outputs.
  • taxsim_names=True renames only those worksheet columns to TAXSIM's labels (credits, v10 to v45, staxbc).
  • keep_intermediate=True also returns every intermediate federal and state column, for auditing.
calculate_taxes(df, idtl=2)
calculate_taxes(df, idtl=2, taxsim_names=True)

docs.title: Calculation mode
docs.text:
calculation_mode Behavior "statutory" (default) Uses the current-law parameter tables and the reviewed corrections to TAXSIM. Use this for new analysis. "taxsim" Reproduces the compiled TAXSIM, known bugs included, for replication and comparison.

You can also pass taxsim_py.CalculationMode.STATUTORY or .TAXSIM. The list of differences is in Statutory corrections.

docs.title: Engine: engine
docs.text:
engine Behavior "rust" (default) The compiled calculator, built into the platform wheels. About 4 to 8 times faster than Python, and it streams, so large files run in far less memory. Statutory mode only: it raises an error for taxsim mode, idtl=2 and keep_intermediate, and for a state or year it has no law for (states from 1977, federal from 1960). It never falls back to Python. "python" The slower, pure-Python implementation. It is the only engine for taxsim mode and detailed output, and the one to use on a platform without the compiled calculator. Always eager.

Both engines give the same statutory-mode results, to floating-point round-off. Set the default for a whole session with the TAXSIM_PY_ENGINE environment variable (rust or python).

The engine also decides laziness. Give engine="rust" a LazyFrame and you get a LazyFrame back: the input plus the output columns (and frate/srate with mtr), a plan nothing has run yet. Collect it, or stream it into any Polars sink so the data never has to fit in memory:

lf = pl.scan_parquet("households.parquet")
calculate_taxes(lf, year=2022, mtr=85).sink_parquet("taxes.parquet")

The year can come from a column (year_column, default "year"), so one pass can cover many years and states. Checks of the data itself (a null or unsupported mstat, years after 2025) raise when the plan runs, and a DataFrame input is checked up front. engine="python" collects a LazyFrame and returns a DataFrame.

docs.title: Speed and memory
docs.text:
Option Meaning batch_rows (Python engine) Maximum input rows per batch. Lower it to cap memory on very large inputs. max_year_workers (Python engine) Threads used to run years and row batches concurrently. The default is Polars' thread pool size (set POLARS_MAX_THREADS to change it).

See Performance for timings and memory.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: calculate_taxes raises ValueError for a missing state, mstat or year column; a null mstat or year; an unsupported mstat; an empty frame; and years outside 1960-2025 (state tax from 1977).

docs.title: Command line
docs.text:
taxsim-py INPUT [OUTPUT]

OUTPUT is optional; without it the result is CSV on standard output.

taxsim-py households.csv taxes.parquet
taxsim-py households.dta                       # CSV on standard output
taxsim-py households.csv taxes.csv --mode taxsim --batch-rows 50000 --workers 4
Flag Meaning --mode {statutory,taxsim} Calculation mode (Calculating). Default statutory. --year YEAR Tax year for every row, instead of the year column. --state-id-type {taxsim,fips} How the state column is coded. --idtl {0,2} 2 adds the detailed federal and state worksheets. --mtr CODE Marginal-rate code (codes). --taxsim-names Use TAXSIM's labels for the detail columns. --keep-intermediate Also return intermediate columns. --lowercase Lowercase the input column names (useful for SAS files). --batch-rows N Maximum input rows per batch. --workers N Threads (batches in flight). --input-format, --output-format Override the file type when the extension is not useful.

Errors print as taxsim-py: message and exit with status 1.

docs.title: File types
docs.text:
The type comes from the extension.

Type Extensions Read Write CSV / TSV csv, txt, tsv yes yes Parquet parquet, pq yes yes Arrow IPC arrow, feather, ipc yes yes JSON lines ndjson, jsonl yes yes Stata dta extra extra SPSS sav, zsav extra extra SAS sas7bdat extra no

"extra" needs pip install "taxsim-py[readstat]", which adds polars-readstat.

docs.title: From Python
docs.text:
The same readers and writers are available directly:

from taxsim_py import calculate_taxes
from taxsim_py.io.tables import read_table, write_table

frame = read_table("households.dta")
write_table(calculate_taxes(frame), "taxes.parquet")

Both take an optional second argument that overrides the file type.

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: The inputs are TAXSIM's, with the same names, meanings and units. Dollar amounts are annual and in nominal dollars of the tax year. Anything absent or null counts as 0, except where noted. Extra columns in your data are carried through to the result untouched.

docs.title: Required
docs.text: Column Meaning year Tax year, 1960-2025. Not needed if you pass year= to calculate_taxes. state TAXSIM state code 1-51 (alphabetical, with DC as 9), or 0 for no state tax. With state_id_type="fips", Census FIPS codes. mstat Filing status: 1 single (head of household if depx > 0), 2 joint, 6 married filing separately, 8 dependent filer. The older codes 3, 33 and 66 are also accepted.

docs.title: Household
docs.text: Column Meaning taxsimid Your case identifier. Optional and carried through. page, sage Age of the taxpayer and spouse (0 if none). Used for age-65 and similar provisions. depx Number of dependents. dep13, dep17, dep18 Dependents under 13, 17 and 18 (child care, child tax credit and similar). Default to depx. dep6, dep19 Dependents under 6 and under 19 (or students). age1, age2, age3 Ages of up to three dependents. If any is present, the age counts above come from these. children_under_3, children_under_4, children_under_7 Optional extensions for survey data. Not part of TAXSIM's inputs; default to 0.

docs.title: Income
docs.text: Column Meaning pwages, swages Wages of the taxpayer and spouse. psemp, ssemp Self-employment income of the taxpayer and spouse. Gets no qualified business income deduction; use pbusinc/pprofinc for that. dividends, intrec Dividends and interest received. stcg, ltcg Short- and long-term capital gains. otherprop Other property income, subject to the net investment income tax. nonprop Other non-property income, such as alimony received. pensions Taxable pensions and IRA distributions. gssi Gross Social Security benefits. pui, sui Unemployment compensation of the taxpayer and spouse. ui is the combined older form. transfers Non-taxable transfers, which count for state benefits tests. scorp S-corporation income. pbusinc, sbusinc Qualified business income of the taxpayer and spouse. pprofinc, sprofinc Qualified business income from specified service trades.

docs.title: Deductions and expenses
docs.text: Column Meaning rentpaid Rent paid (for state renter credits). proptax Real estate taxes paid. otheritem Other itemized deductions, such as state and local taxes, medical expenses and charity. childcare Child care expenses. mortgage Mortgage interest and other deductions that are not subject to the usual limits.

docs.title: Calculation controls
docs.text:
Column Meaning mtr Marginal-rate code per row (see Calculating). idtl 2 for the detailed worksheets on that row.

!!! note Two conventions to know: psemp/ssemp get no qualified business income deduction (use pbusinc/pprofinc), and pensions is treated as the kind of pension each state exempts.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text: The result is your input columns, unchanged and in order, followed by these.

docs.title: Default columns
docs.text: Column Meaning fiitax Federal income tax liability, after credits and including capital gains rates, AMT and surtaxes. Can be negative with refundable credits. siitax State income tax liability. fica Payroll tax: Social Security and Medicare, employee plus employer, plus self-employment tax. tfica The taxpayer's own share of fica. ficar Payroll tax rate (percent). addmed Additional Medicare tax. agi Federal adjusted gross income. taxable_income Federal taxable income. taxable_unemployment Unemployment compensation included in federal AGI. earned_income Earned income. regular_tax Federal regular income tax, before credits and AMT.

docs.title: Year outputs
docs.text:
Provisions that exist only in some years have a default column that appears only when the input includes one of those years. Rows from other years show 0. The columns returned therefore depend on the years supplied: stacking the results of separate runs can leave nulls where one run lacks the column.

Column Years Meaning recovery_rebate_credit 2020-2021 Recovery rebate credit (Economic Impact Payments), refundable.

docs.title: With mtr
docs.text: Column Meaning frate Federal marginal rate, percent, with respect to the chosen income. srate State marginal rate, percent.

docs.title: With idtl=2
docs.text:
Descriptive names; taxsim_names=True swaps in the label in the right-hand column.

Federal

States that do not use a line report 0 for it, as TAXSIM does.

docs.title: Performance
docs.text: The default engine is the compiled calculator. On a mixed 42-state batch of one million rows, including marginal rates, it takes 0.46 seconds and 1.1 GiB RAM, against 17.3 seconds for the Fortran TAXSIM and about 45 seconds for PolicyEngine's TAXSIM runner on only 15,000 rows. A lazy input streams into any Polars sink with memory that depends mainly on the thread count and hardly on the number of rows. Results depend on the data and hardware.

docs.title: Comparison with TAXSIM and PolicyEngine
docs.text:
Tax year 2022, 42 states, taxes and weighted-wage marginal rates. Each cell shows runtime and peak memory for a single first call in a fresh process, with 16 Polars threads and default settings:

Model 1,000 10,000 15,000 100,000 200,000 500,000 1,000,000 taxsim_py, rust (default) 0.03 s165 MiB 0.03 s174 MiB 0.03 s178 MiB 0.07 s258 MiB 0.12 s353 MiB 0.24 s638 MiB 0.46 s1,103 MiB taxsim_py, Python engine 0.88 s341 MiB 1.09 s445 MiB 1.16 s508 MiB 2.15 s706 MiB 2.55 s960 MiB 4.07 s1,821 MiB 7.13 s2,893 MiB Fortran TAXSIM 0.03 s4 MiB 0.18 s4 MiB 0.27 s4 MiB 1.78 s4 MiB 3.53 s4 MiB 8.87 s4 MiB 17.32 s4 MiB PolicyEngine TAXSIM 19.61 s2,306 MiB 32.81 s5,940 MiB 44.77 s8,034 MiB — — — —

Memory is peak process RSS (for Fortran TAXSIM, its executable only). PolicyEngine's runner hit the 8 GiB memory budget at 15,000 rows and larger runs were stopped, so those cells are dashes.

docs.title: Streaming a file
docs.text: calculate_taxes(pl.scan_parquet(path), year=2022, mtr=85).sink_parquet(out) runs the same plan without loading the file. On 4 million rows without marginal rates (about 1.0 s, 1.6 GB with 16 threads) and 16 million rows (3.3 s, 2.6 GB), memory depends mainly on the number of Polars threads (it grew from 1.6 GB to 2.6 GB for four times the rows): with POLARS_MAX_THREADS=8 the 16 million rows take 3.7 s and 1.4 GB, and with 4 threads 6.0 s and 0.76 GB.

docs.title: Memory
docs.text: With the default engine, memory is set mainly by the Polars thread count: set POLARS_MAX_THREADS before importing Polars to trade speed for memory (see the streaming numbers above). For files larger than memory, pass a LazyFrame and sink the result.

docs.title: Comparison with PolicyEngine-US
docs.text: taxsim_py in statutory mode is compared with PolicyEngine-US's TAXSIM API for the federal return and all 45 income-tax states, tax years 2022-2025. It is a cross-check, not an assertion that PolicyEngine is the reference: where the two disagree, the form or statute decides, and the cause is listed below.

docs.title: Method
docs.text:
• Synthetic grid. Both models see identical, explicit inputs: single and joint filers, income from $0 to $1.5M, 0-2 children with explicit ages, age-65+ households (pension-only, Social Security-only, interest-only), itemizers and renters. Rows where federal tax differs by more than $1 are dropped so only state logic is compared; a row is "off" when state tax differs by more than $1.
  • CPS ASEC samples give a realistic income mix but are noisier, because PolicyEngine's adapter ignores dep6 and turns dep13/dep17 counts into children of default ages, so credits keyed to a child's age are compared against the wrong child.
  • The PolicyEngine run disables state and local tax deductions (disable_salt=True) and one-time rebates are removed with a twin simulation.

docs.title: Result
docs.text: The federal return matches on every grid row. Most states are exact on the grid in all four years; the rest differ only for the reasons below.

docs.title: Remaining differences, and why
docs.text:
State Difference Cause (who is right) DE, HI taxsim-py itemizes at middle incomes TAXSIM imputes a sales-tax itemized deduction; PolicyEngine's run has none. The gap is the deduction times the rate (larger in 2025 with the $40,000 SALT cap). Federal Self-employment income (psemp) gets no 20% business deduction TAXSIM applies the qualified-business-income deduction only to the business-income inputs (pbusinc, pprofinc); PolicyEngine also applies it to self-employment income. taxsim-py keeps TAXSIM's convention. Federal Social Security tax when transfers is present TAXSIM counts transfers as tax-exempt interest in the Social Security provisional-income test; the independent models do not treat ordinary transfers that way. taxsim-py keeps TAXSIM's convention. Federal nonprop TAXSIM includes it as income; mapping it to Tax-Calculator alimony can exclude it after 2018. ID Exactly $10 taxsim-py includes the Permanent Building Fund tax (2024 Form 40, line 32); PolicyEngine omits it. CO Rebate amounts PolicyEngine includes the TABOR cash-back rebate; one-time payments are deliberately left out. ME, OR Rebate amounts Maine affordability payment and Oregon kicker are one-time payments, left out. Maine rent is assumed to exclude utilities. MO, MT Pension-only rows PolicyEngine treats TAXSIM's pensions as a private pension; the port follows TAXSIM's convention (the single input is the kind each state exempts). KS Food sales tax credit Refundable in the statute; PolicyEngine treats it as nonrefundable. taxsim-py follows the statute. VA Low-income credit plus EITC PolicyEngine pays both; the 2023 Form 760 instructions allow one. taxsim-py follows the form. NY $16-$33 child credit PolicyEngine uses the current federal child credit; Form IT-213 uses 2017 federal rules, which the port follows. NJ Pension exclusion at $125,000-$150,000 PolicyEngine applies the phase-down to the pension; the statute applies it to the maximum exclusion. IN EITC, one joint row PolicyEngine pays 10% of the current federal credit but gates eligibility on frozen 2023 rules. WA Capital gains excise tax Not modelled: TAXSIM's ltcg cannot separate the exempt real-estate and retirement gains. The Working Families credit is modelled and exact. MN, MA, VT, WI Renter / homeowner refund tables PolicyEngine differs or lacks the inputs; the Minnesota tables are unvalidated. KS, MS High-income itemizers Small residuals, not traced. AR Low-income tables, $1.6 recapture detail, joint return with one earner at about $30,000 PolicyEngine applies the main schedule where one spouse has all the income; taxsim-py applies the joint low-income table. CA Joint at $600,000 with children ($91-$280); single childless at $250,000 ($6) Exemption-credit phase-out details, not traced. CT Rows on the $1,000-or-part exemption phase-out boundary TAXSIM adds $0.001 to AGI. MD, ME, IL $180,000 and above Small residuals.

Provisions TAXSIM has no input for are not modelled in either direction: deductions for tips, overtime and car-loan interest (2025), 529-plan and military-retirement items, county and local rates, and foster-youth or residency eligibility.

docs.title: Federal 2025 (P.L. 119-21)
docs.text: Child credit $2,200; senior deduction ($6,000 per person 65+, reduced 6% of income over $75,000 / $150,000, not for married-separate); SALT cap $40,000, reduced 30% of AGI over $500,000 to a $10,000 floor. States that start from federal income either conform or add these back (ID, IA, MT, AZ, SC; ME and DC keep the pre-2025 standard deduction).

docs.title: Sources
docs.text: State parameters come from PolicyEngine-US's parameter tree, checked against the state forms and instructions where the two were unclear. Corrections that differ from TAXSIM are recorded in Statutory corrections.

docs.title: Using taxsim-py from Stata
docs.text:
taxsim_py is a Stata command that calculates taxes for the data in memory with the same input and output variables as NBER's taxsim35. If you already use taxsim35 or taxsimlocal35, change the command name and your do-file should run. Nothing is sent to a server: the calculation runs on your computer, inside Stata's own Python.

It needs Stata 16 or newer.

docs.title: Install
docs.text: There are two parts: the Stata command, and a Python environment with taxsim-py that the command uses. You do both once.

docs.title: 1. Install the command
docs.text:
Every release has a Stata zip. The address below always gives the newest release:

https://github.com/jrothbaum/taxsim_py/releases/latest/download/taxsim_py-stata.zip

To install a particular version, use that release's taxsim_py-stata-vX.Y.Z.zip instead, for example .../releases/download/v0.4.0/taxsim_py-stata-v0.4.0.zip.

Stata's net install cannot read a zip, so unzip it first, then install from the folder. This does both from inside Stata:

copy "https://github.com/jrothbaum/taxsim_py/releases/latest/download/taxsim_py-stata.zip" ///
    "taxsim_py_stata.zip", replace
mkdir taxsim_py_stata
cd taxsim_py_stata
unzipfile "../taxsim_py_stata.zip", replace
net install taxsim_py, from("`c(pwd)'") replace

You can also download and unzip the file in a browser, then give net install the folder that holds taxsim_py.pkg.

The release zip is the recommended route. To follow the development version instead, install straight from GitHub (Stata needs the raw-file address of the stata folder, not the web page):

net install taxsim_py, from("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jrothbaum/taxsim_py/main/stata") replace

help taxsim_py then shows the full syntax.

docs.title: 2. Install the taxsim-py Python library
docs.text:
The command does the calculation with taxsim-py, a Python library, so that must be installed too. Stata runs Python through its built-in Python integration (help python); it needs Python 3.9 or newer, which python query shows. If Stata has none, you can install one with uv, which is also used below (install uv). In a terminal:

uv python install
uv python find --no-project     # prints the path to that Python

Then point Stata at the path that uv python find printed, as described in Stata's own instructions (help python, or setting up Stata to use Python). Any other installation, such as one from python.org, works too; on Windows it must be an installed Python, not the python.exe inside a virtual environment.

The easiest way is to let the command build a Python environment for you. It uses uv, a free, fast Python package manager, so uv must be installed (see above). Then run, in Stata:

taxsim_py install, path(folder)

This creates the environment in the folder you name (it must not exist yet, or be empty) and installs taxsim-py into it. You can use it immediately, with no restart. For later sessions, the command prints the set python_userpath line that makes Stata find it again; run it at the start of a session (or put it in your profile.do).

If you already manage your own Python environment, install taxsim-py into it yourself, with the readstat extra, which lets it read and write Stata .dta files:

uv add "taxsim-py[readstat]"

Then make Stata use that environment; taxsim_py install, path(<that folder>) changes nothing in it and prints the Stata lines to run.

docs.title: Update or pin a version
docs.text:
taxsim_py install, path(folder) update          // newest release
taxsim_py install, path(folder) version(x.y.z)   // a specific release, such as 1.2.3

Restart Stata afterwards if the current session had already used taxsim-py. install only changes environments that it created.

docs.title: If something is missing
docs.text: taxsim_py checks everything before it calculates. When Python cannot start, taxsim-py or polars-readstat cannot be imported, or taxsim-py is too old, it stops and prints the exact setting to change.

docs.title: Calculate
docs.text:
Load your data, then run taxsim_py. You must say what to do with the results: replace merges them into the data in memory on taxsimid, and saving() writes them to a file.

use households, clear
taxsim_py, replace
summarize fiitax siitax fica

If the data have no taxsimid, one is created from the observation number. year and mstat are required; state is 0 (no state tax) when absent, and absent dollar amounts are 0. Variable names are TAXSIM's, listed under Inputs. Input variables must be numeric; a missing value is an error unless you add missing_to_zero.

The results are fiitax siitax fica frate srate ficar tfica, with taxsim35's variable labels. See Outputs.

docs.title: An example
docs.text:
NBER's test case, a married couple with $100,000 of long-term capital gains in 1970:

clear
input state year mstat ltcg
0 1970 2 100000
end
taxsim_py, full interest replace
display fiitax        // 16700.04

docs.title: Options
docs.text: Option Meaning replace Merge the results into the data in memory, replacing existing output variables. saving(filename) Write the results to a file. The extension sets the type: .dta (with labels), .parquet, .csv, .tsv, .arrow, .ndjson or .sav. Add , replace to overwrite. full Also return the detailed federal and state worksheets, v10 to v45. secondary, wages, interest, long, mortgage Which income or deduction the marginal rates frate and srate are for. The default is the primary earner's wages. backwards_compatible Reproduce TAXSIM's own calculation, errors included. See below. missing_to_zero Treat missing input values as 0. threads(#) Number of threads. Takes effect only on the first call in a session; afterwards set POLARS_MAX_THREADS before starting Stata.

docs.title: Statutory law or TAXSIM
docs.text:
By default taxsim_py calculates under current statutory law and corrects the places where TAXSIM departs from it (the corrections). Add backwards_compatible to reproduce TAXSIM exactly, for example to compare with results you already have from taxsim35. That mode is slower, because it runs the pure-Python implementation.

taxsim_py, replace backwards_compatible

docs.title: Good to know
docs.text:
• The first call in a Stata session takes about a second to start Python; later calls are fast. For how long the calculation itself takes, compared with the Fortran taxsim35 program, see Performance.
  • Results can differ slightly from taxsim35 at very high incomes, because taxsim35 rounds values when it writes and reads its CSV files and taxsim_py does not.

docs.title: TAXSIM errors and corrections
docs.text:
This page lists the apparent errors in NBER TAXSIM that turned up while porting it, what taxsim-py does about each one, and the other deliberate differences from the compiled program. Each error was judged from the Fortran source and from tests against the compiled program. None has been confirmed with TAXSIM's authors.

Line numbers refer to taxsim_2024_09_21.f, and "the executable" means taxsim2024.exe.

The taxsim-py column says how each error is handled:

  • Statutory: calculation_mode="statutory", the default, follows the law, and calculation_mode="taxsim" reproduces TAXSIM for replication and oracle tests. Each correction has an ID and a switch, named in the row, in src/taxsim_py/behavior.py; formula code reads that profile, never the mode string. Tests are rows of tests/statutory_correction_table.py, run by tests/test_statutory_corrections.py (federal payroll tax: tests/test_calculation_modes.py). Years after 2021 run only in statutory mode for states, so a fix confined to those years needs no switch.
  • Both modes: TAXSIM's number is wrong or out of date for its year, so the published value is used in both modes, as for parameter updates (new years, dated tables). scripts/validate_states.py counts these state years as expected differences (KNOWN_ORACLE_DIVERGENT_STATE_YEARS); scripts/validate_federal.py marks the federal cases oracle_divergent.
  • Projection: the error is in TAXSIM's projection of 2021 law to later years. Taxsim mode keeps it; statutory mode uses actual law for those years.
  • No effect and Not changed: the error cannot change a result, or the right rule needs information TAXSIM has no input for.

Every entry needs a reason, an implementation reference, and tests for both behaviors. Differences that are not TAXSIM errors (extensions and actual law for 2022 on), how the executable processes a file, and entries found not to be errors are listed at the end.

docs.title: Federal marginal rate that states read
docs.text:
Some states before 2001 (Nebraska, North Dakota, Rhode Island and Vermont report it as their bracket rate) use TAXSIM's analytic federal marginal rate (comnew(72)). These errors affect only that rate, not federal tax. Statutory mode corrects each, FED-RATE-001 (correct_analytic_federal_rate), except the Social Security term: the branch TAXSIM always takes there is the correct formula, and the alternative it skips would count the EITC slope twice.

docs.title: Other differences from TAXSIM
docs.text:
These are statutory-mode differences that do not fix a TAXSIM error.

  • WA-001 (extension). TAXSIM calls no Washington tax routine, so state tax is 0. Statutory mode adds the Working Families Tax Credit (RCW 82.08.0206), a refundable $300-$1,290 by number of children, phased out below the EITC ceiling with a $50 floor, as negative state tax, through 2025. The 7% capital gains excise tax over $250,000 is not modelled: TAXSIM's ltcg cannot separate the exempt real estate and retirement gains. PolicyEngine taxes all ltcg, so large-gain households differ by about 7% of the gain above the threshold. Switch: add_washington_working_families_credit.
  • CT-001 (2022+). The personal-credit worksheet is read as discrete AGI bands (the first threshold reached), not TAXSIM's linear interpolation between rows (2022 CT-1040 instructions).
  • OR-002. The 12% under-three EITC match uses children_under_3, and the care credit cap uses dep13.

docs.title: Dated 2022+ state tables (STATE-DATED)
docs.text:
TAXSIM's tables stop at 2021 and its later years scale 2021 law. Statutory mode runs actual law for 2022-2025 from PolicyEngine-US parameters checked against state forms; taxsim mode keeps the projection. Boundaries are the provisions TAXSIM has no input for (see the PolicyEngine comparison).

State (IDs) Dated values AR (AR-001) Standard deduction, rate and subtraction schedules, low-income tax tables, 2022-2023 inflationary-relief credit CA (CA-003) Standard deductions, rate thresholds, exemption credits, CalEITC maximums, Young Child Tax Credit amounts, AMT exemptions and phaseout starts (Schedule P (540)) DC (DC-001) Schedule H maximum, AGI tiers, elderly threshold; rent counts at 20% added to property tax HI (HI-002) 2024 doubled standard deductions, 2023-2024 Food/Excise credit tables, refundable 40% EITC from 2023 (Acts 46, 114, 163) NH (NH-001) Interest-and-dividends rate 4% (2023), 3% (2024), 0 (2025); exemptions unchanged OH (OH-001) Brackets, zero-bracket thresholds, exemptions, 30% EITC match (2024 IT-1040) OK (OK-001) Single/separate and joint/head-of-household rate tables (0.25%-4.75%) OR (OR-001) Brackets, standard deductions, federal-tax-subtraction limits, exemption credits Others CO, CT, GA, ID, IL, IN, KY, MI, NC, PA, UT and the remaining income-tax states: see the PolicyEngine comparison

docs.title: Age-65+ rules in actual-law years (STATE-2022-AGED)
docs.text: Statutory mode only, 2022 onward; each follows the state's form or statute. AZ senior property-tax credit limited to taxes paid (all statutory years, AZ-001); IN elderly credit as a step schedule; NM low-income rebate tables; KY pension cap per spouse (all statutory years, KY-001), combined filing, and poverty-guideline family-size credit; OH joint-filing credit for pension income; NJ pension exclusion phase-down; CA credit for age 65+; MN subtraction for the elderly or disabled; ND marriage credit with shared pensions; MI tier-three standard deduction and phased-in retirement subtraction; CO high-income add-backs; RI $20,000 retirement exclusion from 2023 with indexed limits; WV family credit tested on federal AGI; and smaller items in IA, GA, MT, LA, AR, IL, AL and UT. TAXSIM has one household pensions total, so per-spouse caps and spouse-income tests treat it as split evenly.

docs.title: 2025 (2025-LAW)
docs.text: Federal: child credit $2,200, the senior deduction, and the SALT cap phase-down (src/taxsim_py/parameters/national/*). States: see the PolicyEngine comparison. Provisions that depart from TAXSIM's conventions (Maine's and DC's refusal of the larger federal standard deduction, South Carolina's addbacks) are statutory mode only; parameter updates apply in every mode.

docs.text:
These were logged as possible errors and, on review, match the law.

Entry Why it stands Head-of-household code 3 never occurs (several states) Code 3 always appears with code 6 and sets separate-return halving, so it is a legacy separate-return code. Iowa's larger head-of-household standard deduction is Iowa law.
